nameStory: The name 'radiata' comes from the Latin word for 'rayed' or 'radiating,' referring to the star-like pattern of cracks that radiate outward from the center of this tiny fungus's fruiting bodies. Think of it like a miniature sunburst frozen in time on tree bark. The common name reflects this distinctive radiating appearance that helps separate it from other crusty fungi.
description: Stictis radiata is a small crusty fungus that forms tiny disk-like fruiting bodies on dead hardwood bark. Each fruiting body is only about 1-3 millimeters across - roughly the size of a pinhead - but they often cluster together in groups. The most striking feature is the pattern of fine cracks that radiate outward from the center like spokes on a wheel. This fungus belongs to a group called crustose fungi because they form thin, crust-like growths that are tightly attached to their substrate.

idTips.label: Radiating crack pattern
idTips.description: Look for tiny star-burst or wheel-spoke patterns of fine cracks radiating from the center of each small disk - this is the key identifying feature that gives the species its name

idTips.label: Size and clustering
idTips.description: Individual fruiting bodies are pinhead-sized (1-3mm) but often appear in scattered clusters across the bark surface, creating a constellation effect

idTips.label: Texture and color
idTips.description: The surface feels slightly rough and crusty to the touch, typically appearing grayish-brown to dark brown, sometimes with a slightly lighter colored rim

idTips.label: Substrate preference
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on the dead bark of hardwood trees, particularly smooth-barked species like maple and birch where the tiny disks stand out clearly

idTips.label: Attachment style
idTips.description: The fungus forms a thin crust that's firmly glued to the bark surface - you can't peel it off like you might with some lichens

habitat: Look for this tiny fungus on the dead bark of hardwood trees throughout New England's mixed and deciduous forests. It particularly favors smooth-barked trees like maples, birches, and beeches where its small fruiting bodies are easier to spot. You'll find it from sea level up into the mountains, wherever dead hardwood branches and fallen logs provide suitable habitat.

seasonality.spring: Fruiting bodies become more noticeable as they begin to mature and the radiating crack patterns become more pronounced with spring moisture.
seasonality.summer: This is the best time to spot the distinctive radiating patterns, as the fruiting bodies are fully developed and the cracks are most visible in good light.
seasonality.fall: Still visible and identifiable, though some older fruiting bodies may begin to weather and lose their crisp radiating pattern.
seasonality.winter: Persistent through winter months on protected bark surfaces, though snow cover may make them harder to locate on fallen logs.

funFact: Despite being incredibly tiny, each of those radiating cracks actually represents a natural 'fault line' in the fungus that helps it release millions of microscopic spores - it's like a biological firecracker that splits along predetermined lines to scatter its seeds!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small crusty fungi on bark, but the radiating crack pattern is unique - think 'sunburst cracks' and you'll remember what to look for. Other bark fungi might be crusty or disk-like, but they won't have that distinctive spoke-wheel pattern.
contextualKnowledge: Note that this species is extremely rare in New England with only two recorded observations, so consider yourself very fortunate if you spot one! The rarity might be due to its tiny size making it easy to overlook rather than actual scarcity.
compareHints: Compared to its relative the Can-of-worms Lichen (Stictis urceolata), Stictis radiata has the distinctive radiating crack pattern rather than the irregularly wavy, worm-like surface texture of its cousin. Both are tiny crusty fungi, but the crack patterns are completely different - radiating spokes versus squiggly lines.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Can-of-worms Lichen differs from its relative Stictis radiata by its more cylindrical, worm-like fruiting bodies rather than the flatter, more disc-shaped structures of S.
